source.title: Searching to Exploit Memorization Effect in Learning from Corrupted Labels
source.authors: Hansi Yang; Quanming Yao; Bo Han; Gang Niu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some appendix references are unresolved placeholders, and the detailed setup for Figure 1 is not included.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures training and testing accuracy over training on datasets with several label-noise conditions, bearing on V4. It does not test completely random labels or the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: Figure 1(b) and 1(c) report training and testing accuracy curves for noisy-label settings. The text says training accuracy increases and testing accuracy first increases and then slowly drops. Results cited from Zhang et al. and Arpit et al. are not extracted as this paper's results. No accuracy values are stated in the text, and the detailed setup is deferred to an unavailable appendix.
record.test_reason: Section 3.3.1 reports the authors’ own learning curves and interprets early improvement followed by overfitting as learning signal before memorizing noise. This bears qualitatively on V6. The curves do not establish V4’s perfect training fit or its test-error trend across corruption levels.
record.authors_conclusion: The record’s paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that S2E exploits memorization through an expressive, compact schedule search space and an efficient search algorithm, outperforming compared noisy-label methods and selecting a higher proportion of clean samples.
record.recipe_differences: Measures training and testing accuracy during noisy-label learning, rather than fitting completely random labels and comparing to true labels under otherwise unchanged settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Figure 1 varies dataset, label-noise type and level, architecture, optimizer, and optimizer settings; the text says the training/testing accuracy pattern is independent of architecture, optimizer, and hyperparameter choice.

fits_no_version.finding: S2E improves test accuracy, clean-sample selection precision, and search efficiency relative to competing methods.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Automated sample-selection schedules can improve learning with noisy labels.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: Figure 1 values are presented only in plots; no exact values are stated in the text. The referenced detailed setup is in an unavailable appendix. The experiments cover selected noise levels, not a complete sweep from no corruption to all labels corrupted.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1(b) and 1(c) show accuracy curves, but the text gives only qualitative trends and the supplied text does not include the detailed setup. No result rows were extracted from the plots.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Time to fit random versus real labels and how convergence changes with corruption fraction.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit across corruption fractions and steadily increasing test error toward chance as corruption rises from none to all. Increasing accuracy over training does not establish these results.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Separate learning trajectories for clean and corrupted training examples, and a direct comparison of real-label and completely random-label learning.

missing.what: The authors’ qualitative phase interpretation and reported robustness across architectures, optimizers, and optimizer settings bear on V6 but are not represented as results. The omitted training/test curves themselves are already declared in rows_left_out. Exact accuracy values and phase boundaries cannot be recovered from the supplied text.
missing.locator: Section 3.3.1, Figure 1(d–f), and the subsequent observations describing early pattern learning and later memorization.

record.verdict_notes: The record overlooks the authors’ own qualitative evidence relevant to V6 and overstates coverage of V4. No rows were supplied to correct. The supplied text contains figure captions and narrative descriptions but no readable plotted values; it does not justify claims of perfect training fit.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, chance test error, and fitting without changing architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training time to fit random versus true labels and convergence as corruption rises.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.

The paper reports curves for selected corruption levels, but does not state that training error remains perfect, cover corruption from none to all, or report a steady rise in test error toward chance. Figure-only curve values are not transcribed as exact measurements.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation affect random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
The paper cites prior work for learning easy patterns before noisy samples; it does not itself measure whether real and random labels are learned differently over training.

relationships.condition: Qualitative learning dynamics on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 with symmetric 20%/50% and pair 45% label noise.
relationships.reason: Based on Section 3.3.1 rather than extracted rows: training accuracy increases while test accuracy initially improves and subsequently declines; the authors interpret these phases as early pattern learning followed by noise memorization. This is indirect evidence without separate clean/noisy fitting measurements.
relationships.display_finding: Training accuracy increased while test accuracy initially improved and later declined, which the authors interpreted as early pattern learning followed by noise memorization.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
